report:
**Conclusion: The claim is false.** The large body of high-quality scientific evidence shows no link between the number of childhood vaccines and autism.

**Key evidence:**

1. **DeStefano et al. (2013, Journal of Pediatrics)** — a CDC-conducted case-control study of ~1,000 children directly tested whether the cumulative number of vaccine antigens (a proxy for "how many vaccines") given in the first two years of life was associated with autism risk. It found no association, even though today's schedule includes more vaccines than decades ago (https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(13)00666-5/fulltext; corroborated by NPR's coverage: https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2013/03/29/175626824/the-number-of-early-childhood-vaccines-not-linked-to-autism).

2. **Taylor, Swerdfeger & Eslick (2014, Vaccine)** — a meta-analysis pooling data from over 1.2 million children across multiple cohort and case-control studies found no association between vaccination (including total number of vaccines, MMR, and thimerosal/mercury exposure) and autism or autism spectrum disorder (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/).

3. **Institute of Medicine (2004)**, an independent expert panel convened by the National Academies, reviewed the epidemiological evidence and concluded it "favors rejection of a causal relationship" between vaccines (MMR and thimerosal-containing vaccines) and autism (https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10997/chapter/2).

4. **Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health** summarizes why experts across numerous independent studies—varying vaccine type, dose count, and ingredient—consistently found no relationship between vaccine quantity and autism risk (https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism).

**Note on recent controversy:** In late 2025, CDC revised its website to suggest the claim is not fully settled; however, independent fact-checkers found this revision misrepresented the underlying research (https://www.factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/). The peer-reviewed evidence remains consistent: vaccine quantity does not increase autism risk.
